newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli bonds end higher on inflation hopes.
newsitem.headline: Israeli bonds end higher on inflation hopes.

text.p: Israeli unlinked bonds, spurred by expectations of declining inflation, led a broad rise in bond prices on Sunday, traders said.
* Unlinked government bonds (Gilon -- issued for four years): +0.35 pct to 171.02.
* Bank of Israel short-term Makam bills: +0.21 pct to 161.43
Volume was moderate at 154 million shekels with most of the activity concentrated in unlinked bonds and Makams.

"The positive trend in the bond market continued today becuause investors are predicting that inflation will be relatively low next year. In the end, the Bank of Israel will also be forced to lower its key lending rate," said Amir Eayal at Epsilon Securities.
"Investors are predicting that the Bank of Israel will decide to lower the interest rates soon after the government approves the budget cuts," said Gila Shkury of Israel Discount Bank.

The Treasury is now preparing two billion shekels in second-round 1997 budget cuts to present to the cabinet next Monday on top of the 4.9 billion shekels already being sought. Parliament has until December 31 to approve the entire 1997 budget.
"Unlinked bonds were the main gainers today. They are very attractive because the interest rate is relatively high and inflation is expected to decline," Eayal said.

Traders noted that unlinked bonds were also rising because of strong demand from the mutual funds that specialize in unlinked bonds. These funds tend to sell bonds before the end of the month to enjoy certain tax benefits and then buy them back at the beginning of the month.
Makams also rose because of hopes for lower inflation.
Traders said activity in inflation-linked bonds was a low 32 million shekels. "The rise in CPI-linked bonds today was a technical correction following their decline last week," Shkury said.
Dollar-linked bonds rose in response to the recent rise of the dollar against the shekel, Shkury added.
Note: Makams are zero-coupon unlinked certificates with durations of three months to one year. The Bank of Israel issues Makams to absorb liquidity.
